rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: **Linear expansion definition:** When a solid is heated, its length increases. The fractional increase in length per unit rise in temperature is called the coefficient of linear expansion, $\alpha$.  ·  **Formula:** $\Delta L = L_0 \alpha \Delta T$, where $L_0$ is the original length, $\alpha$ is the coefficient of linear expansion (unit: K⁻¹ or °C⁻¹), and $\Delta T$ is the temperature change.

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: **New length:** $L = L_0(1 + \alpha\Delta T)$. For small $\alpha\Delta T$, this is an excellent approximation. For large temperature ranges, $\alpha$ may vary and must be treated as a function of temperature.  ·  **Physical origin:** Heating increases the amplitude of atomic vibrations in the lattice. Because the interatomic potential is asymmetric (steeper on the compression side), the average separation increases with temperature, causing expansion.  ·  **Coefficient of linear expansion for common materials:** Steel: $\alpha \approx 12 \times 10^{-6}$ K⁻¹. Aluminum: $\alpha \approx 24 \times 10^{-6}$ K⁻¹. Copper: $\alpha \approx 17 \times 10^{-6}$ K⁻¹. Invar (Fe-Ni alloy): $\alpha \approx 1.2 \times 10^{-6}$ K⁻¹. Quartz: $\alpha \approx 0.5 \times 10^{-6}$ K⁻¹.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: State the limit / condition where a formula or rule stops being valid before applying it.  ·  **Why metals expand more:** Metals with weaker interatomic bonds (larger bond length, lower melting point) tend to have larger $\alpha$. Lead ($\alpha \approx 29 \times 10^{-6}$) expands more than steel because its atomic bonds are weaker.  ·  **Bimetallic strip:** Two metals with different $\alpha$ bonded together bend when heated — the higher-$\alpha$ metal expands more, forcing the strip to curve. Used in thermostats, circuit breakers, and temperature indicators.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: **Railway tracks — expansion gaps:** Steel rails expand by $\Delta L = L_0 \alpha \Delta T$. For a 12 m rail and $\Delta T = 40°C$: $\Delta L = 12 \times 12 \times 10^{-6} \times 40 = 5.76$ mm. Gaps are left between rails to accommodate this expansion, otherwise buckling occurs.  ·  **Measuring $\alpha$ — Searle's apparatus:** A metal rod is heated uniformly. The expansion is measured by a micrometer screw gauge. $\alpha = \frac{\Delta L}{L_0 \Delta T}$. The apparatus minimizes errors from thermal expansion of the frame.  ·  **Measuring $\alpha$ — Hoke's apparatus:** Uses a glass tube filled with liquid. As the solid rod inside expands, it displaces liquid. The volume of displaced liquid gives $\Delta L$ indirectly. This is an elegant optical-mechanical method.
